params.question: Which of the following best describes the clinical framework for deciding when ECT is indicated?

answers.text: ECT is indicated only after at least two antidepressant trials have failed over a period of 12 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is too narrow. Pharmacological failure is one of three pillars, but ECT may be a first-line option when the clinical situation is urgent (e.g. imminent risk from refusal to eat) or when drugs themselves are contraindicated.

answers.text: ECT is indicated when the clinical situation demands urgency, when pharmacotherapy has failed, or when pharmacotherapy is contraindicated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This three-part framework — urgency, pharmacological failure, and pharmacological contraindication — prevents both under-use (by recognising ECT as first-line in emergencies) and over-use of the treatment.

answers.text: ECT is reserved exclusively for treatment-resistant schizophrenia once all antipsychotic options have been exhausted

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ECT is not limited to schizophrenia, nor does it require exhausting all antipsychotics. Its indications span severe depression, catatonia, severe mania, and situations where pharmacotherapy poses an unacceptable risk.

answers.text: ECT is indicated primarily when the patient or family specifically requests it as a treatment option

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Patient or family preference does not determine ECT indication. Indications are evidence-based clinical decisions driven by urgency, pharmacological failure, or contraindication to drug therapy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three-pillar framework: ECT is indicated when (1) the patient cannot safely wait for drugs to work, (2) adequate pharmacotherapy has already failed, or (3) pharmacotherapy itself is contraindicated.
Well done. The urgency–failure–contraindication framework is the clinical logic that governs all ECT indications and prevents both under-use and over-use.

params.question: A patient undergoing a course of ECT reports difficulty recalling her daughter's wedding that occurred two months before treatment began. Which type of memory disturbance does this represent, and what is its most likely prognosis?

answers.text: Anterograde amnesia; it is likely to be permanent and untreatable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anterograde amnesia is difficulty forming NEW memories during the treatment course, not recalling past events. This patient's difficulty is with a pre-treatment memory, which is retrograde amnesia.

answers.text: Retrograde amnesia; it will most likely resolve within weeks to months after the ECT course ends

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Difficulty recalling events that occurred BEFORE ECT is retrograde amnesia. The majority of ECT-related memory effects are transient and resolve within weeks to months, though a minority of patients may experience persistent gaps for events close to the treatment period.

answers.text: Retrograde amnesia; it invariably indicates structural hippocampal damage requiring neuroimaging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ECT-related retrograde amnesia does not indicate structural brain damage. It is a functional and usually transient cognitive effect, not evidence of hippocampal injury. Neuroimaging is not routinely indicated for this expected adverse effect.

answers.text: Anterograde amnesia; it will resolve immediately once the current ECT session ends

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This scenario describes difficulty with a pre-treatment memory (retrograde amnesia), not difficulty forming new memories (anterograde). Additionally, memory effects do not resolve after a single session — they typically improve over weeks to months after the full course.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: retrograde amnesia = difficulty recalling events BEFORE ECT; anterograde amnesia = difficulty forming NEW memories DURING treatment. The majority of both types resolve within weeks to months after the ECT course ends.

Excellent. Distinguishing retrograde from anterograde amnesia and knowing that most effects are transient is essential for accurate informed consent discussions and for countering exaggerated fears about ECT.
